docs.title: Start here
docs.text: SKRCTF is a free platform where you learn cybersecurity by solving hands-on challenges. Each solved challenge gives you a flag, a secret text you submit for points.

docs.title: Your first 30 minutes
docs.text:
1. Create your account — 5 min
  2. Solve your first challenge — 15 min
  3. Learn the webshell — 10 min

Then follow the Beginner pathway.

Stuck?

Being stuck is normal. Players who rated challenges "very challenging" made the most attempts, and kept going. See What the data says.

docs.title: Style guide
docs.text: Rules for anyone writing SKRCTF learning docs.

docs.title: Every page
docs.text:
• Opens with Goal and Time (or Who).
  • Ends with Done when and a Next link.
  • One task per page.

docs.title: Writing
docs.text:
• Plain English. Short sentences, under 25 words.
  • Second person ("you"), active voice.
  • Explain a term the first time it appears.
  • Never give away a flag or a full solution in onboarding pages.

docs.title: Formatting
docs.text:
• Numbered lists for steps, tables for comparisons.
  • Code and commands in backticks.
  • Use admonitions: tip for advice, warning for common mistakes.

docs.title: Claims
docs.text: • Any number must cite its source.

docs.title: Review
docs.text: Every change goes through a pull request and one review before merge.

docs.title: Write-up template
docs.text:
Copy this when sharing how you solved a challenge.

# <Challenge name>

**Category:** <e.g. Forensics>  **Difficulty:** <Easy / Medium / Hard>

## What the challenge gives you
<Files, links or description in one or two lines>

## Approach
1. <First thing you tried and why>
2. <What worked>

## Tools used
- <tool> — <what for>

## What I learned
<One or two lines>

Do not paste the flag itself.

docs.title: What the data says
docs.text:
These findings shape how SKRCTF's learning pathways are ordered.

Source: Khoo, L. J. et al. (2024). Analyzing Performance Patterns and User Experience in Online Cybersecurity Challenges: Insights from SKRCTF. International Journal of Multimedia & Its Applications, 16(6), 1–12. Study of 120 learners (aged 19–30) across 127 challenges, 2024 cohort.

docs.title: Completion rate by category
docs.text:
Tier Category Completion Entry OSINT 83.3% Entry Warm up 54.5% Entry Forensics 47.2% Entry Linux 44.6% Intermediate Steganography 35.4% Intermediate Cryptography 33.5% Intermediate Web 29.8% Intermediate Binary 29.2% Advanced Misc 14.2% Advanced Programming 12.5%

Design decision: the Beginner pathway starts with entry-tier categories.

docs.title: Analytical before technical
docs.text:
Challenge type Average completion Analytical (Forensics, OSINT, Crypto, Stego) 46.7% Mixed (Warm up, Linux, Mini games, Misc) 36.7% Technical (Web, RE, Binary, Programming) 28.0%

Design decision: analytical challenges are the entry point; technical ones come later with more guidance.

docs.title: More attempts is not always better
docs.text:
Players with 101–150 attempts had the highest completion rate (52.1%). Beyond that, extra attempts added little.

Design decision: docs encourage regular, measured practice instead of grinding.

docs.title: Hard does not mean quit
docs.text:
Perceived difficulty correlated negatively with score (r = −0.421). But players who rated challenges "very challenging" made more attempts (107 on average) than those who found them easy (73).

Design decision: docs label difficulty honestly and normalise being stuck.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text: Single cohort, self-reported difficulty, no long-term follow-up.

docs.title: 1. Create your account
docs.text:
Goal: an activated account and a team, ready to play. Time: 5–10 minutes.

Solo or team, everyone follows the same steps

SKRCTF scores by team. Even if you play alone, you must create a team.

  1. Register. Go to skrctf.me and select Register. Sign up with your name and email.
  2. Activate your account. Open the email from SKRCTF and click the activation link. (check spam/junk folder)
  3. Create a team. Log in and create a team, even for solo players.
  4. Share your team password (only if teammates are joining). They use it to join your team. Keep this credentials for webshell later.

Common mistakes

  • No activation email? Check your spam folder.
  • Skipping team creation: you cannot submit flags until you have a team.

Full visual guide on the platform: skrctf.me/guide

Done when: you are logged in and can see your team on the Teams page.

Next: Solve your first challenge

docs.title: 2. Solve your first challenge
docs.text: Goal: submit one correct flag. Time: 15 minutes.

docs.title: What is a flag?
docs.text: A flag is a secret string hidden inside a challenge. It usually looks like 7h1s_15_7h3_Fl@g. Finding it proves you solved the challenge. However, you need to submit the flag as SKR{7h1s_15_7h3_Fl@g} across SKRCTF unless specified.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Open Challenges and choose the Warm up category.
  2. Pick the challenge with the lowest difficulty. Challenges are ordered from easiest to hardest.
  3. Read the description and download any attached file.
  4. Find the flag and paste it exactly into the box, then select Submit.

Common mistakes

  • Extra spaces before or after the flag
  • Wrong capital letters — flags are case-sensitive
  • typo errors - I vs l vs 1, 0 vs O
  • Sharing flags: some flags are unique per player, so a copied flag will not work

Done when: the challenge shows as solved.

After solving, read other players' write-ups for that challenge to see different approaches.

Next: Use the webshell

docs.title: 3. Use the webshell
docs.text:
Goal: run Linux commands in your browser. Time: 10 minutes.

Some challenges need a Linux terminal. SKRCTF gives you one in the browser, so you do not need to install anything.

  1. Open Webshell from the menu.
  2. Log in with the GROUP credentials shown on your profile page.
  3. Try these commands:
Command What it does ls List files cat file.txt Show a file's contents nc host port Connect to a challenge server

Done when: ls runs without errors.

Next: Beginner pathway

docs.title: Beginner pathway
docs.text: Goal: your first 10 solves, in an order that builds confidence. Who: new players with no CTF experience.

docs.title: Why this order
docs.text: Player data shows analytical challenges (Forensics, OSINT, Crypto, Steganography) have a 46.7% completion rate, against 28.0% for technical ones (Web, Reverse Engineering, Binary, Programming). So start analytical, then move to technical. See the data.

docs.title: Stage 1 — Get comfortable (solves 1–4)
docs.text: Category Why Warm up Learn how flags and submission work OSINT Highest completion rate (83%): research skills, no tools needed Forensics Look inside files and find hidden data

docs.title: Stage 2 — Build patterns (solves 5–7)
docs.text: Category Why Linux Practise the webshell Cryptography Recognise common encodings and ciphers Steganography Find data hidden in images and audio

docs.title: Stage 3 — First technical steps (solves 8–10)
docs.text: Category Why Web Inspect and change how websites behave Binary Your first look at how programs run

docs.title: How to practise
docs.text:
• Steady, regular sessions beat long bursts. The most effective players made 101–150 attempts across the platform, not the most attempts.
  • After each solve, read one other player's write-up.
  • Pick a direction after Stage 3: go deep in one category (specialist) or broad across many (generalist). Both work.
